stories.headline: Why did Man City fans bring inflatable bananas to Anfield?
stories.summary: At Anfield on Sunday, Man City fans waved hundreds of inflatable bananas, but how do they relate to the club's guilty verdict?
stories.body:
Back in Premier League action for the first time since being found guilty of serious financial rules breaches, Manchester City entered the pitch against Liverpool to a predictably hostile reception from the Anfield faithful.

With accusatory banners unfurled, boos audible, and chanting reverberating around the stadium, many of the traveling City fans decided to put on a defiant display of their own with one particular aspect of their matchday counter-protests raising quizzical eyebrows among onlookers -- namely, the large number of inflatable bananas being wielded among the away section.

While looking like an ostensibly odd choice to those unaware, it was not a spur-of-the-moment call -- nor is it a recent phenomenon. In fact, City fans have actually been taking inflatable bananas to games since the 1980s.

Indeed, the practice dates back to the 1987-88 season in particular. Having been demoted down into the English second tier from the old First Division the previous season, it's said that one match-going City fan decided to lighten the atmosphere at Maine Road by taking a large inflatable banana along to a game.

It also happens that the club had a popular striker by the name of Imre Varadi playing for them at the time. Varadi spent two seasons with City during his nomadic career, in which time he acquired the affectionate nickname "Imre Banana" on the terraces. This led to a rise in the number of inflatable bananas showing up in the crowd at Maine Road -- the practice quickly caught on and has endured, if fairly intermittently, for almost 40 years.

Bananas were relatively commonplace at City matches during the 1980s and '90s though the fad did appear to phase out during the modern era, following the club's stadium change and takeover in the mid-2000s. However, Sunday's heated faceoff with rivals Liverpool saw the trend revived as hundreds of yellow plastic effigies were seen bobbing around in the Anfield Road Stand.

So, while City were busy being lambasted as "cheats" from all four corners of Anfield and being threatened with potential relegation, their fans were waving bananas around as a slightly eccentric homage to their days in the lower leagues.

stories.headline: Making sense of the Giants-Commanders tie, the Texans' Marvin Harrison Jr. trade
stories.summary: What were the Commanders doing in the final minute of OT? Why did the 1-4 Texans make an aggressive trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.? Let's find try to find the logic.
stories.body:
Two very different decisions -- one on the field and another off it -- had me asking the same question by Sunday afternoon on Week 5: What are they thinking?

There were the Commanders, who bizarrely decided to run the clock late in overtime against the Giants in field goal range and saw the game end without ever getting a chance to attempt the game-winning kick. And there were the Texans, who won their first game of the season and celebrated by making a surprisingly aggressive move on offense, trading second- and sixth-round picks to the Cardinals for a seventh-rounder and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., who has underwhelmed during his pro career so far.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

I love trying to explain the inexplicable, so let's give it a shot. Why did a 1-4 Texans team -- whose playoff chances sit at 23.2% after Sunday's victory, per ESPN's Football Power Index -- trade a significant future pick to acquire a player at a position where it already has Nico Collins? And what on earth were the Commanders attempting to do at the end of that game?

I'll try to answer both those questions today, starting with the decision to try to kick-start a frustrating season by trading for one of the league's most frustrating players.

Jump to:

The 1-4 Texans traded for Harrison?

The Commanders let the clock expire?

The Texans' trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.
Of course, the simple explanation for why the Texans traded for Harrison starts with one simple argument. We're about two and a half years removed from Harrison entering the 2024 NFL draft as arguably the most exciting and polished wide receiver prospect of his generation. Even amid a legendary run of Ohio State wide receivers that includes the likes of Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Chris Olave, Garrett Wilson, Emeka Egbuka and others, Harrison was seen alongside Jeremiah Smith as the two best pro prospects of the bunch.

Our various draft analysts saw Harrison as no worse than the third-best player overall in the class of 2024. There just aren't many players with Harrison's sort of scouting reports and college pedigree to ever enter the league. They don't come available via trade very often, and it's even rarer to get a shot at acquiring them just after they turn 24 years old.

The Texans have been through this under general manager Nick Caserio and don't regret their decision in the past. After drafting C.J. Stroud with the second pick of the 2023 draft, the Texans surprised everyone by trading two first-round picks and a second-rounder to the Cardinals to move up for edge rusher Will Anderson Jr. with the third overall selection. It was a move that seemed overly aggressive for a team that projected to be among the worst in football the following year, but it turned out to be a masterstroke.

The Texans were a playoff team with Stroud and Anderson, with the latter emerging as one of the most dominant defenders in all of football. Like Anderson, Harrison plays a premium position. And while we don't have access to Houston's scouting reports, this trade implies that it saw Harrison as a potential superstar entering the league after his run at Ohio State. Stroud, Harrison's college teammate with the Buckeyes, gave a glowing report to the organization and said that the wideout was "probably the hardest worker I've ever been around in my life."

The difference, of course, is that in Anderson, the Texans were trading up for a player with a great college résumé who hadn't yet played at the pro level. With Harrison, the Texans are trading for a player who has been outright disappointing as a pro over a multiple-season sample. He isn't a bad player, but he has hardly been great. Since 2024, he ranks 70th out of 130 wideouts in yards per route run (1.54) and 44th in receiving yards per game (47.8). He hasn't had great quarterback play, but Harrison has been roundly outperformed by Trey McBride and Michael Wilson within the same offense.

On one hand, Harrison's contract is extremely affordable, which is important for a Texans team that just paid Anderson and has deals for Stroud, Calen Bullock and Kamari Lassiter to come over the next 12 months. Harrison will make just $776,000 over the remainder of 2026 and $5.6 million in 2027. Even if the Texans decide to pick up Harrison's fifth-year option in 2028, that deal projects to come in at only $17.2 million.

That's a total of $23.6 million over the next three years, which is just a tiny bit more than what Jakobi Meyers is making per year on his existing contract. That number rises if you factor in the surplus value of the draft picks sent to the Cardinals, which throws another $33 million onto the pile -- but even $56.6 million over the next three years would be reasonable WR2 money right now. It'll look even cheaper as the cap rises over the next two seasons.

The Texans are obviously counting on Harrison delivering something more than solid WR2 performance and living up to his lofty predraft expectations. Will he get there? To answer that question, there were two places to look. First, I wanted to get a sense of why Harrison was struggling in Arizona to see whether a change of scenery might be likely to unlock the second-generation pro. Second, I looked back through history to find examples of highly drafted players turning things around in a second act with a new team.

What went wrong in Arizona?

The simplest answer is the one that Texans fans would fear the most. While there are mitigating factors and potential excuses to be made, the reality is that Harrison just wasn't able to get himself open often enough to get the sort of target share or rack up the sort of receiving production his draft status suggested was coming. While anyone with access to All-22 film and a lot of free time can undoubtedly find plays where he was open and didn't get the football, that's also true for any starting receiver in football.

During his time with the Cardinals, Harrison ranked last in the NFL among all wide receivers (with 50 targets or more over the past three years) in separation, averaging just 2.1 yards of separation when targeted, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Great receivers -- even ones that get plenty of attention from opposing defenses -- are typically able to create more space for themselves. The likes of Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson average over 3 yards of separation on their routes. In Arizona, McBride averaged 3.3 yards of separation on his targets during that time, while Wilson was at 2.5 yards.

In part because of those separation issues, Harrison didn't have a lot of chances to bring in easy targets. His expected catch rate over the past three years, using the Next Gen Stats model, was only 53.7%. That's fifth-lowest among wide receivers since the start of 2024. I'll get to the four below him in a minute.

By those expectations, the good news is that Harrison has roughly delivered about what the model would project given that low expected catch rate. He has caught 53.5% of his passes so far as a pro, almost exactly in line with the model's prediction. He has generated a total of 34 receiving yards over expectation across his 202 targets, which is also essentially a match for what the model suggests. You could make a case that Harrison has done an average job with below-average opportunities and hope that his expected catch rate will rise in Houston.

But my concern is that Harrison is not separating because he hasn't been explosive enough. The four other wideouts with lower expected catch rates are Alec Pierce, Tyquan Thornton, Marquez Valdes-Scantling and Christian Watson. Those are all deep threats who primarily make their money with their speed and ability to get open downfield. While they're going to draw targets that don't have great chances of being caught, the huge gains those receivers provide when they do bring in the football make up for the low catch rates.

Next Gen Stats also tracks speed, and given their route trees and athleticism, those guys unsurprisingly spike. Pierce hits at least 18 mph on 17.6% of his routes. Thornton's at 18%, while Watson gets there just under 20% of the time. Valdes-Scantling isn't on their level, but he's also in his 30s.

Harrison tops 18 mph on just 3.1% of his routes, which is both far below those players and way below the league average for qualifying wide receivers (6.5%). He has topped 20 mph on routes just four times as a pro, a shockingly low number for a player who topped 22 mph at the college level. Max speeds can be a product of the routes each receiver is called upon to run, but Harrison has been in the NFL long enough to run the full route tree.

If you try drilling down on the subset of players who both don't create a lot of separation (2.5 yards or less) and don't hit top speeds very often (getting over 18 mph on less than 4% of their routes), it's not a very promising group. There's Harrison and eight other players, most of whom aren't impactful NFL starters at this point of their careers. That list includes Keon Coleman, Gabe Davis, (very late-era) DeAndre Hopkins, David Moore and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine. Jauan Jennings is a better version of that player, but he also provides significant value as a blocker and after the catch.

The two exceptions are a pair of contested-catch stars in A.J. Brown and Mike Evans, players who create explosives for themselves by physically dominating defensive backs and create space by threatening those big plays and working back to the quarterback. That's the way Harrison probably has to succeed given his play style.

Those two are just much better at it than Harrison has been. Brown catches more than 54% of the tight- and neutral-window throws (3 yards of separation or less) in his direction that travel more than 10 yards in the air, the fourth-best rate in the league. Evans is at 49%. Harrison's at 40.2%, which is below the league average of 42%. And while quarterback effects could factor in there, both McBride (42.4%) and Wilson (45.7%) caught a higher percentage of downfield throws into tight or neutral windows than Harrison, all while getting open far more often in other situations.

So, in short, Harrison hasn't created much separation, isn't reaching the sort of NFL-level speed we associate with young wide receivers very often and hasn't been even average in contested or neutral catch situations downfield. His drop rate (5.0%) is worse than league average. And while his quarterbacks aren't award winners, just 16.4% of the throws in Harrison's direction have been off-target, which is lower than the league average of 20.6%.

Given those constraints, Harrison has generally done solid work. But he wasn't supposed to have those constraints. He was supposed to be a complete prospect, capable of running past players, outmuscling them or (most often) separating from them with elite route running. He hasn't done any of that consistently as a pro over a multiyear, multi-QB, multi-scheme sample. That has to be concerning given our expectations for him heading into the NFL.

Defenses weren't treating him like the guy they needed to stop in Arizona. At the end of the 2025 season, when the Cardinals played the Bengals, Cincinnati took top cornerback DJ Turner II and stuck him on Arizona's top wide receiver for the vast majority of the game. Only to the Bengals, that player was Wilson, not Harrison. Double-coverage rates are often exaggerated by announcers and fans (who often conflate a safety playing over the top as a double-team or bracket coverage on a specific player), but Next Gen Stats records only one true case of Harrison being double-covered over his first three seasons in the league.

Are there things the Cardinals could have done to make Harrison's life easier or factors that might influence those numbers? Probably, yes. Harrison was pressed at the line on 31.5% of his snaps, the 17th-highest rate in the NFL over the past three years. That might prevent Harrison from getting to top speed or creating easy separation as often as he might like. But there are also plenty of players who were pressed more often than Harrison who haven't had those issues, ranging from superstars such as Chase and Jefferson to role players such as Romeo Doubs and Kayshon Boutte. Nico Collins, Harrison's future teammate, has been pressed at the line on more than 37% of his routes over the past three years and has been far more productive.

Arizona also ran one of the more static offenses in football for most of Harrison's time with the Cardinals, using motion at one of the lowest rates in the game. Harrison has just four catches over three seasons on plays where he was put in motion before the snap or as it was imminent, producing a total of 39 receiving yards. The Texans use motion at the fourth-highest rate under offensive coordinator Nick Caley.

The Cardinals also rarely used Harrison in stacks and bunches during his time in Arizona, which can help prevent defenses from getting hands on receivers at the line and create communication issues on the defensive side. Harrison has run 26 routes out of stacks over his career, with just three of his 108 catches (2.8%) coming out of a pre-snap bunch. Zay Flowers, who has a league-leading 477 receiving yards over the past three years out of bunch looks, has caught about 16% of his passes as a pro out of stacks. About 11% of the catches by Texans wideouts over the past two years under Caley have come out of bunches.

These are the sorts of things I usually bring up as ways to make life easier for a receiver in his early-30s who might have lost a step and needs some help creating separation. It's not what I typically say about 24-year-olds, let alone first-round picks who were supposed to be as complete and impressive as Harrison was entering the NFL. To believe that Harrison's going to become that player, you have to basically believe that he's going to catch, move and run like a completely different player in Houston than the one we saw in Arizona.

I'm willing to believe that's possible given how high the hopes were for Harrison coming out of school. I just wanted to see whether anyone else had been able to pull this off in the past. Is there a meaningful track record of elite prospects who changed teams early in their careers and thrived in their new landing spots?

What does history tell us about the Harrison trade?

Teams typically don't want to move on from first-round picks this early in their careers, particularly if they're top-10 picks. In recent years, that's partly a product of how contracts are funded, with many first-rounders receiving most of their guaranteed money in an up-front signing bonus, leaving their teams with minimal cash to pay out over the remainder of their deals. The Cardinals, for example, paid $22.5 million of Harrison's $35.4 million rookie deal in a signing bonus before his pro career began. With just $12.9 million due over the next four years, even marginal performance from Harrison would typically be enough to justify a roster spot.

Still, players do get moved. We've seen two top-10 picks from the 2024 draft moved before the end of their third seasons in the NFL over the past two weeks alone, with Harrison (No. 4) dealt to the Texans and quarterback J.J. McCarthy (No. 10) shipped to the Giants. It's obviously too early to judge how those trades panned out. But what about the other times teams have traded away a top-10 pick before the end of his third season in the league? Have they been able to live up to their draft status in their new home?

The most famous example of an early-career trade leading to stardom in a second stop is Steve Young, who struggled with the Buccaneers before thriving with the 49ers. He doesn't fit here for a couple of reasons. One is that he was the first overall pick in the 1984 supplemental draft as opposed to the college entry draft. And while Young played only two seasons with the Bucs, he spent the 1984 season in the USFL before finishing the 1985 and 1986 seasons in Tampa, meaning he completed three full years before joining the 49ers.

Leaving aside other supplemental picks, players who were traded because they were suspended or players who were traded because they were holding out for more money, I can find 12 top-10 selections since 1980 who were dealt away before the end of their third season as a pro. None of them made it to a single Pro Bowl in their new homes or at any other point over the remainder of their careers. Those 12 players are:

McCarthy was just dealt to the Giants and made his debut in Sunday's tie with the Commanders.
QB Trey Lance lost his starting job via injury in 2022 and was deposed by Brock Purdy's emergence as the long-term answer in San Francisco. He was traded to the Cowboys for a fourth-round pick and has made two spot starts over the past two seasons (only one of which was in Dallas).
CB C.J. Henderson started just 10 games with the Jaguars before the Urban Meyer regime that inherited him dealt the 2020 ninth overall pick to the Panthers. Henderson has mostly been a reserve cornerback since then, although he's in the middle of his best year as a pro with the Falcons.
QB Josh Rosen was the 10th pick in the 2018 draft and didn't play well in his debut season with the Cardinals, leading Arizona to use the top pick the following year on Murray. Rosen was dealt to Miami during the 2019 draft for a second-round pick and started three more games with the Dolphins before retiring after the 2022 season.
CB Eli Apple was traded midway through his third season from the Giants to the Saints, where the 2016 top-10 pick was a solid starter on a 13-win team. Apple has bounced around the league and played regularly for the Bengals team that made it to the Super Bowl in 2021, but he was never able to convince another franchise to keep him around on a multiyear deal.
CB Justin Gilbert (eighth pick in 2014) was traded by the Browns after two nondescript seasons to the Steelers, where he spent one year as a reserve before violating the league's substance abuse policy. He never returned to the NFL.
LB/S Mark Barron (seventh pick in 2012) wasn't a great fit for Lovie Smith's scheme in Tampa and was traded in the middle of his third season to the Rams for two Day 3 picks. The linebacker/safety tweener started for several years with the Rams without ever making it to a Pro Bowl.
RB Trent Richardson, the third overall pick of the 2012 draft, might be Harrison's closest parallel as a college star who never really seemed to reach those same heights as a pro. The Browns traded him after just 17 pro games to the Colts for a first-round pick. Richardson was out of the league by the end of his third season as a pro.
LB Aaron Curry was regarded as one of the safest prospects in the 2009 class, but he wasn't able to make an impact in Seattle and was dealt before the end of his third season to the Raiders after losing his starting job to K.J. Wright. Curry didn't turn things around in Oakland and played his final two games with the Raiders in 2012.
Edge rusher Gaines Adams' case is much sadder. He was traded to the Bears midway through his third year in the league after being selected with the fourth overall pick in the 2007 draft, but Adams suffered a cardiac arrest during the offseason and tragically died at the age of 26.

Mike Williams is the lone wide receiver on this list and one of many wideouts with that name. This Williams was the 10th overall pick out of USC in the 2005 draft after sitting out the entire 2004 season. He caught just 37 passes over two years with the Lions before being dealt to the Raiders during the 2007 draft. Williams then spent two years out of football before joining the Seahawks in 2010, where his 65-catch season was enough to finish second in Comeback Player of the Year voting. A broken ankle the following year brought Williams's career to a close.
CB Bruce Pickens started eight games over two-plus years with the Falcons before being thrown in as part of the (lesser-known) Eric Dickerson trade. He started one more game as a pro.
LB Mike Junkin was compared to Lawrence Taylor by Browns scouts before the 1987 draft, but he was traded after two seasons to the Chiefs and was out of the game a year later.

You have to go back to the 1970s to find top-10 picks from the college draft who were traded early in their careers and thrived elsewhere. Ahmad Rashad might be the best-case scenario for Harrison as the fourth overall pick in the 1972 draft. He spent two years with the Rams before being dealt to the Bills, missing a year with a knee injury and then emerging as a four-time Pro Bowler with the Vikings. Ken Burrough was also traded after one year before making two Pro Bowls in the 70s with the Oilers. But we're talking about an entirely different era of football in terms of scouting and player movement.

This isn't a big sample, and in the case of someone like Steve Young, it's absolutely fair to point out that a highly regarded player changed situations after a disappointing start and eventually emerged as a Hall of Famer. We just don't see teams willing to trade away top-10 picks very often, and when we do, it's often because the team that has seen them in practice and on game day every week doesn't think they're all that good.

The Texans would still get some utility out of Harrison if he settles in as a solid receiver, which seems like the most likely scenario. At his modest salary, even WR3-level production wouldn't be a disaster for the Texans over the next couple of years. Houston also gets the rest of the season to evaluate him before deciding on his fifth-year option, which would allow the team to save paying out that 2028 salary if Harrison doesn't meet its expectations.

If Harrison is just an ordinary, nondescript second or third wideout behind Collins, though, the opportunity cost will feel more painful for Caserio. The Texans still haven't solved their offensive line and run game issues, and as their young stars get more expensive, it's going to be more difficult to surround them with veterans on both sides of the ball. That Day 2 pick could have yielded a lineman or allowed them to trade for a high-end veteran like Joe Thuney (who was dealt for a fourth-round pick in 2025). It could have landed a long-term replacement for Dalton Schultz or a running back to finally fill what has been a problem position for years.

It's always good to add talent, but wide receiver wasn't high on Houston's list of needs. And while bringing in receiving help can make life easier for the run game, I'll remind you that the Texans traded a second-round pick in 2024 for Stefon Diggs, hoping that the former Bills star would give them a dominant second option next to Collins. Diggs' brief run with the Texans ended after eight games due to a knee injury, but the offense struggled both with and without him in the lineup -- mostly because the run game and offensive line were among the worst in football.

Had the Texans made this move in August after Jayden Higgins tore his ACL, it would have made a lot of sense. They were a team with championship expectations after three consecutive seasons with a postseason victory. They desperately needed to surround Stroud with as much talent as possible after a difficult run in the playoffs, if only to help build the young quarterback's confidence back up. With a perennially elite defense, building a solid offense gave the Texans a real chance at competing for the top seed in the AFC.

At 1-4, that case is much more difficult to make. Stroud has been excellent this season and seems to have his confidence back, playing well even when Collins was sidelined by a hamstring issue. The Texans have seen their playoff odds drop by 34.3% from the preseason via the Football Power Index, and while they have the league's second-easiest slate of opponents from here on out, they're already pretty far behind the likes of the Chiefs and Jaguars in the AFC. They've also been a middling defense, although Anderson and Co. just delivered their best game of the year in blowing out the Titans.

I can't fault the Texans for taking this swing. This might be Houston's chance to land a Hall of Fame-caliber talent as he enters the prime of his career. Harrison's still a tantalizing prospect, and he's young enough to still look back at the college tape and scouting reports and essentially throw away everything that happened in Arizona. History and Harrison's work with the Cardinals just suggest that the sort of dramatic turnaround the Texans are hoping to see is a long shot.

The Commanders' mismanagement of the final minute of OT
If you want to know how much of a disaster the end of this game was for the Commanders, ask the Giants. After coming back from 14 points down in the fourth quarter, the Giants were in position to win this game in overtime, only for running back Cam Skattebo to fumble in field goal range. A stunned Giants team then allowed 51 yards on the next four plays, pushing the Commanders into position for their own game-winning field goal with 55 seconds to go.

After those seconds came off the clock and the tie was confirmed, Giants defenders celebrated like they had just won the Super Bowl. John Harbaugh, who actually has won a Lombardi Trophy, might not have been any less ecstatic. "I wanted to get off the field before they could take it away from us," said Harbaugh, describing the tie like it was free money he found on the ground. If the Giants could have fit the stadium's goalposts on the plane back to New Jersey, you get the feeling that they might have torn them down before leaving.

The Commanders, of course, felt every bit as rotten after the late-game scenario played out. Having watched it quite a few times, let's try to lay out what did (and did not) happen to get a sense of what went wrong for Jayden Daniels & Co.

With 55 seconds to go, the Commanders were facing a first-and-10 on the Giants' 26-yard line. The Commanders were obviously already in field goal range for rookie Drew Stevens, but amid rainy conditions, this had been an adventurous game for kickers. Stevens missed the opening extra point of the game wide left, while Giants kicker Dominic Zvada had missed field goal attempts from 46, 50 and 57.

You would hope that Stevens would be able to make a 44-yard attempt if the Commanders didn't get any additional yardage, and given that Skattebo had just fumbled while the Giants were in position to kick a 42-yard field goal, there had to be some trepidation on the part of coach Dan Quinn and first-year offensive coordinator David Blough. The Commanders could have essentially kneeled twice and brought Stevens on for a field goal here while draining the clock and preventing the Giants from getting the ball in case of a missed kick. Instead, they elected to try to pick up additional yardage.

Rachaad White runs for 2 yards

Nothing wild here, as the Commanders run a simple shotgun handoff to White for 2 yards. With 50 seconds on the clock as White's tackled, the Commanders don't need to be in any sort of rush. If they want to run the clock down as much as possible, they can line up, kneel inside of 40 seconds on second down on Stevens' preferred hashmark, spike the ball again with several seconds left on third down and then kick on fourth down to win the game.

The Commanders want more yards, which seems aggressive. Their operation is slow and complicated. They change personnel from 11 to 13, getting two tight ends on the field. They huddle up for the playcall. In this window, it's absolutely essential for Blough or whoever else is talking to Daniels to remind the quarterback of the game situation. The Commanders are out of timeouts. Daniels can't take a sack, and given that we know the Commanders are choosing to throw the ball, the pass either needs to be incomplete or to someone who can immediately get out of bounds.

By the time Daniels gets back to the line of scrimmage, there are 17 seconds left on the game clock. Blough's playcall includes motion from the tight end, which takes another four seconds. By the time the Commanders snap the ball, the game clock is down to 12 seconds. There's no way they can run the ball with enough time to reliably spike it on the next snap.

The operation leading to this final play was a disaster. There's no reason the Commanders even needed to run another offensive play, let alone a pass play. It's absolutely the wrong time to be changing personnel and calling a play that requires pre-snap motion. There are too many moving parts that could both go wrong and require attention with the game on the line, distracting the quarterback from managing a unique game situation. Was the playcall Washington got to really better than running inside zone or whatever run concept Blough likes most out of 11 personnel with 30 seconds left on the game clock and spiking the ball afterward?

The Commanders snap the ball with 12 seconds left and chaos ensues

Passing the ball in this situation isn't in itself a disaster, although it wouldn't be my first choice. The Giants had been zero blitzing Daniels throughout the game to try to force sacks or quick throws. With the proper instruction, this play isn't a disaster. Daniels takes the snap and looks toward tight end Ben Sinnott in the flat, but Kayvon Thibodeaux has dropped into coverage and takes away his throwing lane. That's not the end of the world. Throw the ball away over Sinnott's head, stop the clock and kick the field goal.

Very clearly, the information that needed to be conveyed to Daniels was not passed along before communication cut off with 15 seconds to go on the play clock. Daniels does not play out this sequence like someone who knows time is at all of the essence, likely because he believes the Commanders still have a timeout. After the throw to the flat is taken away, Daniels doesn't throw the ball away or look toward any of his other receivers. He goes to tuck and run with the ball to pick up an extra yard or two, making it back to the line of scrimmage.

Daniels even stays down for a second or two after the tackle before he realizes what has happened, which isn't the action of someone who knows that the Commanders need a miracle spike to stop the clock. Blough's playcall also doesn't help matters here, as two of Washington's receivers are 14 yards downfield by the time Daniels takes the 0-yard sack. They need to floor it back to the line of scrimmage, line up correctly and give Daniels enough time to spike the ball to have any hope of winning the game. While they realize something's up, they're barely back on Washington's side of the ball before time expires.

In an ideal world, you would love it if your starting quarterback was aware of the game and timeout situation and knew to throw the ball away to stop the clock in that situation. That's harder than it seems, especially when the Commanders were suddenly marched onto the field by a fumble and had been moving the ball ever since without a timeout. (It's worth nothing that the broadcast, which included a former NFL veteran on color commentary, was advocating for a run with 18 seconds left and also didn't realize what was wrong until after Daniels went down.) There's a reason Daniels took responsibility after the game. He's partially to blame.

Of course, there's also a reason Quinn took responsibility after the game, too. It's his job to make sure that the big-picture game management decisions are communicated appropriately, even if that's as part of a conversation between Blough and Daniels. Handling a situation like this might be as much about preparing during the offseason as it would be in the moment. Blough's a first-time offensive coordinator in his fifth game calling plays. Daniels is a wildly talented quarterback, but this was his 27th start as a pro. Quinn also used a timeout on defense 36 seconds into overtime after an incomplete pass by the Giants, which was one of the reasons the Commanders didn't have one to finish the game here.

It's a disaster. The Commanders weren't guaranteed a victory if they had just kneeled, spiked and attempted a field goal given the conditions on the ground, but they gave up a chance to even attempt that game-winning kick out of sheer sloppiness and poor decision-making, all to run a play to target their third-string tight end that Daniels seemingly wasn't prepared to execute.

In my opinion, this isn't the sort of mistake that should get Quinn fired, but it's right up there with the Tyrique Stevenson Sr. Hail Mary in this same building as the sort of late-game disaster that ends up being tied to a coach as a primary memory after he has lost his job. It's a tie that feels like a loss and a fiasco that will linger in the minds of Commanders fans for years to come.

stories.headline: Toto Wolff finds quirky solution to Kimi Antonelli track limits 'stress'
stories.summary: Toto Wolff joked he would shove a pillow under the a--e of Kimi Antonelli before hailing the Italian's maturity as he moved within reach of the world championship.
stories.body:
Toto Wolff joked he would shove a pillow under the a--e of Kimi Antonelli before hailing the Italian's maturity as he moved within reach of the world championship.

Antonelli claimed third place under the lights in Singapore on Sunday to stretch his advantage in the drivers' standings to 102 points ahead of Mercedes teammate George Russell.

That opens the possibility that the 20-year-old could confirm his place as Formula 1's youngest world champion at the next round in Texas in a fortnight. As things stand, he would need to win at the Circuit of the Americas with Russell ninth or lower and Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower.

Antonelli's dominance of the season has been remarkable, especially given his difficult debut campaign last year, and he is all-but certain to clinch his place in the sport's history books over the next few races.

He has, though, proved that he has a penchant for pushing track limits. He again received a final warning for the violation in Singapore, as he has done on several occasions this season, with one more fault leading to a penalty.

Mercedes boss Wolff has a solution as he admitted it causes tension on the pit wall.

"I have a good strategy, I'm going to put a pillow from the hotel under his a--e, under his butt, so he can actually see the road," Wolff said.

"Because I think it's like this, you know, he can't see it [the track].

"So yeah, under his a--e so he can see, and it stresses us. Half the race we already have three strikes, but it also shows that he's pushing the limits a lot."

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Red Bull downplay 'team to beat' label by George Russell, Oscar Piastri

- Lando Norris takes responsibility for collision with Oscar Piastri in Singapore: 'I let McLaren down'

Antonelli was off the pace for much of the weekend in Singapore but profited from the McLaren pair colliding to take fourth in Saturday's sprint before making late moves to rise from fifth to third in Sunday's main event.

Max Verstappen completed a perfect weekend, backing up sprint victory with a dominant race. The four-time world champion remains 119 points adrift, with Antonelli admitting it would be "very scary" if the Dutchman were in the title fight.

Antonelli was on the radio during the race to ask about issues he felt with the car but battled on to ultimately stand on the podium. Russell recovered to ninth after having to start from the back of the grid.

"I think how he [Antonelli] has driven is mature and good," Wolff added. "We talked about it and he said, 'I've just got to keep my calm here and make sure that I finish the race.'

"So handling a difficult car at that stage and trying to develop it and learn, it's good."

It remains a possibility that the penultimate round in Qatar could be cancelled and the season finale in Abu Dhabi replaced by Imola -- if F1 bosses decide they cannot race in the Middle East due to the ongoing conflict.

If that happened, 25 available points would be off the table, moving the Italian ever closer to the championship.

"I haven't looked at it from that perspective because at the moment I have the thought of how many points is it actually and when could he win it?" Wolff said.

"The aim must be to score points, not to lose too many on the others.

"And then it's going to come towards him. And whether that's in Mexico or Brazil or further down the line, we shall see.

"And I guess whether Qatar and Abu Dhabi happens at the moment, everybody says so. You need to go the direction of this is six more races to go and not four."

stories.headline: Why are Shakhtar playing Champions League games at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge?
stories.summary: Explaining why Ukrainian side Shakhtar Donetsk will play home Champions League games at Chelsea's stadium.
stories.body:
Shakhtar Donetsk will host AEK Athens in the Champions League on Wednesday but the game will be played nearly 1,700 miles from their Ukraine home.

Stamford Bridge, Chelsea's home stadium, will act as Shakhtar's home ground for their European fixtures this season.

ESPN breaks down why that's happening...

Why are Shakhtar playing at Stamford Bridge?

Shakhtar are based in the Ukrainian city of Donetsk.

But they haven't played at their home ground, the Donbas Arena, since 2014. This year, amid security reasons due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, they were seeking a stadium for their four home fixtures in the league phase of the Champions League.

Shakhtar have recently played 'home' European fixtures in Poland, Slovenia and Germany and were linked with using Brentford's stadium this season, but ended up agreeing to play at Stamford Bridge.

FC Shakhtar said: "Playing our Champions League home matches at Stamford Bridge is a special opportunity for Shakhtar. We are grateful to Chelsea Football Club for the opportunity to host our games at this special venue. Stamford Bridge is one of the most famous stadiums in world football, with an incredible history and atmosphere. We are convinced that Shakhtar's matches in London will provide unforgettable emotions for Ukrainian and English fans."

The 2021 UK census states that approximately 19,000 Ukraine-born people live in London.

How does it affect Chelsea?

Chelsea have no European fixtures this season after finishing 10th in the Premier League last season.

The Blues even cited their "disappointing 2025-26 season and failure to qualify for European football" as part of their reasoning to welcome Shakhtar.

A Chelsea statement said: "FC Shakhtar have played in countries across Europe and we look forward to welcoming them to London for their Champions League campaign this year.

"We will be working with the Shakhtar team closely over the coming weeks to ensure that matchdays run safely and smoothly for their team and supporters."

What matches will Stamford Bridge host?

Shakhtar vs. AEK Athens, Oct. 14
Shakhtar vs. Sporting CP, Nov. 3
Shakhtar vs. Fenerbahce, Nov. 25
Shakhtar vs. Real Madrid, Jan. 27

Chelsea were owned by Roman Abramovich

Chelsea were formerly owned by Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich.

He was forced to sell the club after 20 years in 2022 under pressure from UK government sanctions after Russia invaded Ukraine.

Where do Shakhtar play home domestic matches?

Shakhtar have largely played their 'home' matches in the Ukrainian league at the Lviv Arena, which is 600 miles from Donetsk, since 2014.

stories.headline: Windhorst: Why Cooper Flagg's ascension is starting to feel inevitable
stories.summary: The NBA China Games showcased Cooper Flagg's evolving game, leadership and, perhaps most impressive, his franchise-savior ceiling.
stories.body:
MACAO, China -- A few Dallas Mavericks veterans have been keeping up the ruse that Cooper Flagg is still wearing some sort of "trainee" name tag. That the 2025 No. 1 pick is technically a rookie until he plays the first game of his second season.

This played out with various menial duties for the reigning NBA Rookie of the Year -- bag-carrying and the like -- during the team's week in China for two preseason games against the Houston Rockets. "I can sometimes sneak by without them remembering that they want me to be a rookie still. But yeah, they definitely try," Flagg said.

This notion, of course, is ridiculous on its face. Flagg played just 45 minutes in two games in Macao but scored 33 points with 10 rebounds, 10 assists, three steals and two blocks. He hunted for his shot and looked to set up his teammates with the kind of assurance that obliterates the concept that he's a rookie.

But it's not just what you can count or see. Flagg's voice echoed through the arena inside The Venetian Macao, and he's vocally involved in the game, showing how quickly he is graduating from worrying about his own game to broadening his scope by including everyone else's. He's barreling down the runway toward superstardom like the many fully loaded cargo jets taking off from the adjacent Hong Kong International Airport.

This kind of growth creates goosebumps.

"I'm just finding my voice," Flagg said. "Being so young and a little bit inexperienced is tough sometimes, but I think up to this point, I've earned the respect of my teammates, and I've gotten that sense that they really respect me and my opinion."

For a player who has been on the basketball world's radar since he was 16, was a star at Duke and then won the NBA's top rookie honor, it feels possible that Flagg's quickening maturation might be a tad underrated at the moment. It doesn't help that the Mavericks, mired in a deep Western Conference, aren't exactly demanding attention.

But everything about Flagg is starting to feel inevitable.

There's a lot going on in the NBA: LeBron James is in Philadelphia. Giannis Antetokounmpo is in Miami. Victor Wembanyama has claimed the unofficial "future face of the league" designation and is looking for revenge after Jalen Brunson and the New York Knicks, the big-market darlings, grabbed rightful attention by ending their 52-year title drought.

But for a week in Macao for the NBA's China Games, Flagg was the headliner. His image was plastered on the side of buildings and the focus of a big shoe event. Inside one of Macao's glittering high-end, marble-wrapped malls, he unveiled his personal New Balance logo (his initials combined with the silhouette of a pine tree, a nod to his home state of Maine).

This event is more about the business of basketball and branding than the games. NBA commissioner Adam Silver was in town attending meetings with Chinese partners. Flagg's boss, Mavericks owner Patrick Dumont, was the week's host as the CEO of Las Vegas Sands Corp., operator of five resorts in the area with 10,000 combined hotel rooms plus the Venetian Arena, an opulent building that feels like a five-star resort with two hoops.

It's easy to lose focus on the game, but it is still impossible to miss how Flagg appears to be blossoming. He's just 19, still a teenager until Dec. 21, if you can believe it. Actually, taking into account the more polished jumper, the improved footwork and the unmistakable leadership he shows on the court, it's impossible to believe.

"He's going to lead this franchise into the future. You can definitely bank on that," teammate Kyrie Irving said. "He deserves a lot of the praise he's gotten because he's carried a lot. ... He's wise beyond his years."

Flagg, during a 30-second span on Friday, maneuvered through the Rockets defense with a slick sideways jump stop to drill a midrange jumper, blocked Amen Thompson's shot, gathered the rebound and led a fast break that resulted in him throwing down a lob dunk.

A few possessions later, Thompson, playing by the book, went under on a screen while defending Flagg, who he drilled a 3-pointer from the top of the key with ease.

"He's such a versatile player, someone that literally can score three levels," Mavericks first-year coach Dusty May said. "He can make defensive plays on and off the ball."

Here's a refresher of what Flagg accomplished last season:

He became the first rookie to lead his team in total points, rebounds, assists and steals since Michael Jordan in 1984-85.
He became the fourth rookie since the NBA-ABA merger in 1976-77 to average at least 20 points, six rebounds and four assists. The others: Luka Doncic, Larry Bird and Jordan.
He became the first teenager with four 40-point games; the first teenager with consecutive 40-point games; and the first teenager with a 50-point game.
He was sixth in the league on baskets off drives and, per GeniusIQ tracking, brought the ball up fifth most among all frontcourt players.

Basically, Flagg carried the load of a mid-career All-Star, not that of a rookie on a 26-win team.

"I felt at points last year I was going in blind a little bit," Flagg said. "Obviously, I hadn't been through a lot of those experiences before. So, I think just having that this year is a big help. Just feeling prepared, feeling ready. There's a lot less to worry about."

Flagg shot 29.5% from 3-point range last season, a hole in his game that is getting addressed. He worked hard over the summer, with much of that time flanked by Irving, who is returning after missing 19 months because of a torn left ACL. People around the team talk about Flagg's work ethic and competitive nature.

"Your talent only gets you so far; being remembered for your work ethic and how you treated people and also that championship mindset you came in with every day, that's what people hold on to," Irving said.

"For me as a peer, but also as a brother, I look at him as someone that has a world of potential, but also still needs a lot of guidance just like we all do in basketball, a lot of teaching, a lot of knowledge being passed."

Much of that will happen under the spotlight. The Mavericks have 21 scheduled national television games this season, and it's not because they're expected to contend. Irving's return should boost them, but they're still climbing out of the hole that was created with the disaster of the Doncic trade and the failure of Anthony Davis' tenure. There's a reason there's a new coach and a new front office, led by highly regarded president Masai Ujiri.

Ujiri has made it clear that the franchise is committed to keeping Irving with Flagg, who is 15 years younger than the star point guard. Rival front offices question whether Dallas can stick to that plan with roster holes elsewhere and the two stars on different career timelines.

That is certainly a backdrop. But Flagg is now on stage, and he is giving off the vibes that he's ready. As they watch him do it every day, the rest of the Mavs feel it.

"This is a big responsibility to help him in his evolution to being one of the best," May said. "A great player's success is determined by everyone around them. So all of us [being] better teammates, better players, better coaches will contribute to him maximizing his potential.

"We don't take it for granted."

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: The Valkyries' wild path from expansion team to the Finals
stories.summary: Two years ago, the Valkyries didn't exist. Now they're competing for their first title -- here's how they did it.
stories.body:
As a general rule, expansion teams aren't really supposed to be very good right away. Sure, the initial player draft offers a chance to assess the league's potentially undervalued and overlooked players on the off chance of finding a hidden treasure, but from there, contention usually requires a lot of patience: A bunch of losing seasons provide the high draft picks to slowly accumulate talent, with a legitimate chance to contend finally waiting at the end of that long building process.

The Golden State Valkyries apparently missed that memo.

Barely two seasons into their existence, the Valkyries are headed to the WNBA Finals against the Atlanta Dream (Game 1 at 12:30 p.m. Saturday). To get there, they closed out the Las Vegas Aces on the road. This was a matchup that began as a huge mismatch in team pedigree -- the Aces had won three of the past four WNBA titles, while Golden State literally didn't exist two years ago -- if not talent. Instead, it became a changing of the guard, with the league's new contender sweeping aside one of its greatest dynasties.

Exactly how historic are the Valkyries as a recent expansion team? And how have they managed to go from an expansion draft to a Finals appearance in less than two years? Let's dive into five charts that explain Golden State's unprecedented rise.

Going into 2025, it was a bit of a mystery how the Valkyries would end up doing in their first WNBA season. Previously, expansion teams had posted an average winning percentage of .306 with a minus-8.4 net rating (we're not including 1997, the league's first season). If history was any indication, fans could expect Golden State to be one of the league's worst teams out of the gates.

But before Golden State, the league hadn't added a new team since the Atlanta Dream in 2008, meaning a backlog of great players was building up in competition for the same number of total roster spots in the W. (Witness the number of high draft picks who would be waived heading into each season.) Contrary to the historical record, this suggested the Valkyries would be tapping into a vast reservoir of available talent when building the first WNBA expansion squad in nearly two decades.

And that has largely proved to be true. The Valkyries ended up having the second-best first-year winning percentage (.523) of any WNBA club -- trailing only the 1998 Detroit Shock (.567) -- and the best expansion year by both net rating (plus-1.8) and Elo rating (1494). And all they've done since is continued that meteoric rise, to the point that they had the best regular season for a second-year team by all available measures of team quality, and in fact finished with the second-best record in the league -- and best net rating overall -- in 2026.

As a result of their dramatic rise from, well, not having a team at all in 2024 to the league's top net rating in 2026, the Valkyries' odds of winning the WNBA title also have risen dramatically. Going into the season, Golden State looked like a solid pick to return to the playoffs and possibly even win a series (last year's season ended with a 2-0 first-round sweep to the Minnesota Lynx). But contending for the championship seemed like a much taller order -- especially in a crowded field that contained the former champion Aces and Liberty, plus the improved Olivia Miles version of the Lynx, an Indiana Fever team featuring a healthy Caitlin Clark, and the overhauled Dream.

And for the first few months of the season, that seemed about right. The Valkyries were 13-7 through the end of June, one of the better records in the league but still clearly within a five-team logjam below Minnesota and Las Vegas. It seemed as if Golden State were destined to spend all year fighting for razor-thin seeding margins within that group. But since July 1, the Valkyries rattled off a league-best 19-5 record and saw their odds in statistical systems like Elo zoom past those of the presumed-favorite Lynx by the end of the regular season, when the latter hit a late slump. A 5-1 playoff start has only reinforced their status as a serious title threat, and now the early-season underdog Valkyries are statistical favorites to win it all.

If we had to pick a single calling card for the Valkyries' impressive championship bid, it has to be their defense. With a defensive rating of 100.6, they not only led all teams in suppressing opponents' per-possession scoring, but the gap between Golden State and No. 2 Atlanta at 104.5 (3.9 points per 100 possessions) was roughly the same as the gap between Atlanta and No. 7 New York at 108.7 -- or nearly the gap to league average itself, which was 109.1. The Valkyries' difference compared to that league figure (minus-8.5 points per 100) ranked as the sixth-best single-season WNBA defense ever relative to average.

The 2025 Valkyries landed on a number of top-tier defenders through the expansion draft, including Veronica Burton on the perimeter and Temi Fagbenle on the inside, helping Golden State rank fourth on defense right out of the gate under coach Natalie Nakase. But an even more refined version of the team's D came into shape in 2026, with names like Kiah Stokes -- whose block saved the Valkyries in Game 2 against Vegas -- and Gabby Williams joining Burton this season.

The Valkyries' defensive recipe blends a few components. They have one of the better rim protectors in the league in Stokes, which contributes to a league-low 47.8 effective FG% allowed, plus a couple of premier ball hawks in Burton and Williams, which forces opponents into mistakes -- they also ranked No. 2 in turnover rate forced. And opponents don't get many easy transition opportunities against Golden State because the Valkyries play at the league's slowest pace and hardly ever turn the ball over. Nakase was the lead assistant under Becky Hammon for the 2023 Aces when they had one of the best defenses in WNBA history -- and now she's using those lessons to try to dethrone her old team.

Obviously, a team doesn't post the league's best net rating and fight to within a game of the WNBA Finals without star performances, and the Valkyries absolutely got one of those this season from Burton.

The Northwestern alum was originally taken No. 7 by Dallas in the 2022 draft, but the Wings never really gave her much opportunity to earn an expanded role; she started 19 only total games in her first two seasons, averaging a paltry 14.5 minutes over that span before being waived before the 2024 season. After signing with Connecticut midseason, Burton continued to log backup minutes (12.7 MPG) despite improving her scoring efficiency with increased usage.

It wasn't until Burton, left unprotected in the expansion draft, landed with Golden State that she finally found a situation in which she could start -- and she has thrived in the role. Averaging 29.0 MPG as a Valkyrie, Burton has remained one of the league's top defensive guards while also taking a huge step forward as an offensive presence, which earned her Most Improved Player honors in 2025. But the advanced metrics in particular adore Burton for her two-way play; her ability to draw fouls while still taking plenty of 3s; her playmaking (she maintained a 34.5% assist rate with just an 11.9% turnover rate); and her massive on-court impact, which showed up at both ends of the court. Burton finished the season ranked second behind only the MVP A'ja Wilson in both LAKER wins added and win shares.

Burton had help. Led by Williams, who arrived from Seattle as a big-time impact player in her own right, six additional Valkyries beyond Burton had at least 2.5 LAKER wins added; no other team in the league had more than five players crack that barrier, much less if their top star is tossed out. Add in Nakase, the 2025 WNBA Coach of the Year, and the Valkyries are loaded with talent from top to bottom.

As much as we've been extolling the virtues of Burton's game, she hasn't been as effective as usual in the playoffs -- averaging just 9.5 PPG on 35.3% shooting from the field in six games. She has still made her trademark on-court impact; Golden State has a plus-12.4 net rating when she's in the game, 13.3 points per 100 better than when she sits. And in the clutch, she made multiple big shots when Golden State needed her. But her postseason LAKER rating of plus-2.7 points per 100 is markedly down from her mark of plus-7.5 in the regular season.

Luckily for the Valkyries, they've received big performances from some of the other names on the roster -- most notably Williams, who is averaging 22.7 PPG in the playoffs. Another player who has run with an opportunity in Golden State, Williams was always more of a defensive player than a scorer in her previous career stops, but her usage rate this season (29.0%) was a whopping 11.2 points higher than her previous career average, and she's pushing it even higher (to 32.1%) in the playoffs.

Of course, Williams does have a tendency to raise her game in the postseason (where her career scoring average of 14.5 PPG is markedly higher than her 9.3 regular-season figure), but this is taking things to a new level. And the other Valkyries to raise their output significantly in the playoffs are Tiffany Hayes and Cecilia Zandalasini, who both have produced massive LAKER ratings (Hayes is at plus-10.7!) in around 18 minutes per game off the bench.

It should be noted that the Valkyries' run has involved its fair share of gritty wins, surviving Dallas in a win-or-go-home Game 3 to win in the first round, needing some late free throws and a last-second block to take the 2-0 lead over Las Vegas, and then outlasting the Aces in overtime of the semifinals clincher. There's no question Golden State will have another tough assignment taking down Angel Reese and the Dream -- and the league's second-best defense -- to win a title.

But the Valkyries have spent their entire, brief existence defying conventional expectations for expansion teams. Why should the most significant step yet along their improbable path to a championship be any different?

stories.body:
There's a Christmas Eve vibe out there Monday for hockey fans. Yes, three games are on the calendar -- including a matinee for the Panthers and Sabres with the kids off from school -- but Tuesday night is the biggest evening of autumn for puckheads.

It's the 2026 edition of Frozen Frenzy, with all 32 teams in action playing games at staggered start times from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. ET.

But that's Tuesday. There are three games to be contested Monday featuring five playoff teams from last season -- with the lone non-playoff team having won the Stanley Cup in 2024 and 2025.

Florida Panthers at Buffalo Sabres

1 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BUF -108, O/U: 6.5

After breaking the NHL's longest playoff drought last season, the Sabres want to make it two playoff runs in a row. The campaign hasn't gotten off as well as hoped, with a 2-3-0 record and minus-8 goal differential. The visiting Panthers have been beset by injuries to key players -- Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand -- and at 2-1-2 aren't far ahead of Buffalo in the standings. This is a critical early matchup between two teams with big postseason dreams.

Ottawa Senators at New Jersey Devils

7 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | NJ -135, O/U: 5.5

The Senators have been a wagon this season, racing out to a tie for the Atlantic Division lead at 4-1-0. That has been built from the net out, with Linus Ullmark entering this game with a 4-0-0 record, 1.34 goals-against average and .942 save percentage. The Devils took two of three from the Sens last season, but to keep the edge they'll have to be a little stingier in goal prevention. New Jersey is allowing the eighth-most goals against per game (3.5). You can do the math in comparing Ullmark's rate against the Devils'.

Vegas Golden Knights at Minnesota Wild

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MIN -118, O/U: 5.5

Had a few (well, quite a few) bounces gone the Wild's direction in their second-round playoff matchup against the Avalanche this past spring, these two teams would've staged an epic Western Conference finals. As it was, the Golden Knights rolled an injury-beset Avs squad in four games to head to the Cup Final.

Nevertheless, based on early returns in 2026-27, both of these teams should be in the mix for the conference finals again. The Wild have allowed the second-fewest goals per game this season (1.80), while the Knights have scored the sixth most per contest (3.67). So on the macro level, there's your big question heading into this Western showdown: Can Jesper Wallstedt continue to be "the Wall of St. Paul" against Jack Eichel, Mitch Marner & Co.?
